info.title: aiwatcher
info.description: Observability for agent runs: events in, traces and live streams out.

post.summary: Store an image under the digest of its own bytes.
post.description:
The digest is computed here. A content address supplied by the caller is
not a content address, and trusting one would let two different images
occupy the same key.

200.description: These exact bytes were already stored

get.summary: The bytes of an uploaded image.
get.description:
Immutable by construction — the key *is* the digest — so it is cached for a
year. An annotation canvas re-fetching a 2 MB plan on every pan would be the
slowest part of the tool.

parameters.name: image_id
parameters.description: The image's SHA-256

get.summary:
One immutable manifest: its samples, its splits, and every exclusion with
its reason.

parameters.name: split
parameters.description: One side of the split, for a trainer that wants its own file per split.

get.summary: The same export as a COCO document.
get.description:
Generated rather than stored: COCO is a derived view of the vector
annotations, and storing it would be a second copy of the truth that can
disagree with the first. It reads one revision object per sample, which is
paid once per training run rather than once per epoch.

parameters.name: split
parameters.description: One side of the split, for a trainer that wants its own file per split.

get.summary: Every export built from a project, newest first.

post.summary:
Freeze the project as it stands into an immutable, content-addressed
manifest.
post.description:
The reference a training run records is `project@export`. Two exports of an
unchanged project are one export, which is why re-running this nightly is
cheap and why a manifest is a comparison boundary rather than a timestamp.

get.summary:
One image, its revision history, one revision's shapes, and the side of the
split its family is on.

parameters.name: revision
parameters.description:
Which revision's shapes to return. Omitted means the accepted one, then
the newest — what a labeller reopening an image expects to see.

get.summary: The images in a project, newest registration first.

post.summary: Register an image into a project, or correct what is known about it.
post.description:
Re-registering keeps the revisions and the review state: a plan re-submitted
with a corrected `group_id` is a correction, and resetting its labels would
punish the correction.

post.summary:
Open a batch: what it is for, what may be done with it, and where it came
from.
post.description:
Rights, evidence and the Hub pin are decided here rather than per page,
because they are properties of the corpus. `revision` is the one worth
filling in even when it feels redundant: a dataset id is a moving target,
and an import that recorded only the name has recorded provenance nobody
can go back to.

post.summary: Stop a job. What it already registered stays registered.
post.description:
Images are content-addressed, so nothing is half-written; what a cancelled
job does not get is a manifest, which is what stops it appearing as a
completed import.

post.summary: Seal the batch and queue the job that reads it.
post.description:
A 200 rather than a 201: what comes back is a job, and the thing it will
produce does not exist yet. The rights check runs here, before anything is
registered — a claim contradicting what a human recorded about the corpus
is a decision to reverse, not a row to skip — so a 400 from this route is
about the corpus rather than about the request's shape.

Always queue a `dry_run` first from a UI. Six hundred thousand images with
the split key mapped from a filename is not something to discover after the
fact, and a dry run costs the downloads and nothing else.

400.description: Empty batch, wrong project, or rights the curated table contradicts

get.summary:
One import's receipt: what it read, what it registered, what it refused,
and on what terms.
Every published import, newest first.
The rows a job refused, and why.
get.description:
The dead-letter half, and the reason it is a route rather than a field on
the job: an import that rejected four hundred thousand rows cannot put them
in a response, and "read the counts, then page the rows" is the difference
between a diagnosable import and a number.

post.summary: Add one page of rows to an open batch.
post.description:
Number the page when the client can. A numbered append is idempotent —
identical bytes are an acknowledged retry, different bytes for a page
already stored are a 400 naming it — which is what makes a million rows
over a flaky link a thing that can be re-sent rather than reconciled.

400.description: Sealed, out of order, or a page rewritten with different rows

post.summary: Register many images at once, from rows a Flow PHP pipeline produced.
post.description:
The write half of dataset discovery. A hub search says a corpus exists; a
Flow query maps its file listing onto this schema; this registers the
result into a project somebody can draw on.

Two things about the response are worth reading rather than skipping. One
bad row does not fail the batch — `outcomes` names every refusal — and
`warnings` carries the states that *succeed* and still leave the corpus
worth less than it looks: unknown rights, and a group key that gave every
image its own family.

Always `dry_run` first from a UI. Six hundred images with the split key
mapped from a filename is not something to discover after the fact.

400.description: The asserted rights contradict what a human recorded about this corpus

get.summary: One project, with the counts that answer "is there enough data yet".
Every annotation project.

post.summary: Create a project, or replace its description, split policy and label schema.
post.description:
The schema version is re-derived from the classes. An unchanged class list
keeps its version and every accepted revision stays valid; a changed one is
a new version, and the next export names every revision drawn under the old
one as excluded rather than quietly relabelling them.

post.summary: Move an image's review state, and pin the revision an export will read.
Save a drawing.
post.description:
A revision that does not validate against the project's schema is not
stored at all, and the 422 carries every problem rather than the first.
Storing an invalid revision and marking it so would move the decision about
whether a half-drawn door is a training target to whatever reads it next.

422.description: The drawing was refused; `details` holds every problem

get.summary: The public floor-plan corpora, and where to look for more.
get.description:
A dated table this build ships, not a search against Hugging Face or
Roboflow. Those mirrors restate licences wrongly often enough that a live
answer would be worse than no answer, because it would arrive looking
authoritative. Every row links its original.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Free text over name, summary, licence, labels and notes.

parameters.name: usage
parameters.description: The filter that matters: what a commercial model may be trained on.

parameters.name: label
parameters.description: A label kind the corpus has to carry — `doors`, `scale`, `graph`.

get.summary: Where the provider sends the browser back to.
get.description:
Every failure here ends in a redirect rather than a JSON error, because
this is a top-level navigation: whatever this returns is what the person
sees in their browser. The reason travels as `sign_in_error`, which the
panel reads and renders on its sign-in screen.

parameters.name: error
parameters.description:
What the provider sends instead of a code when it refused —
`access_denied` when a user cancelled, most often.

get.summary: Whether this instance has a login, and what to call it.
get.description:
The one route besides the health probes that answers before anybody has
signed in. Without it the panel would have to guess, and guessing wrong
means either a sign-in screen on an instance with no provider or an endless
401 loop on one that has.

get.summary: Start a sign-in: a redirect to the provider.

parameters.name: next
parameters.description:
Where to land after signing in. A path on this application; anything
else is refused rather than followed — see `aiwatcher_auth::safe_next`.

501.description: This instance has no identity provider

post.summary: Sign out.

get.summary: The current caller.
Every conversation the archive holds, newest activity first.
One page of a corpus. Content, so `admin` — the same gate as reading a turn.
get.description:
A corpus an erasure has withdrawn answers 410, exactly as an erased turn
does: its manifest, counts and digests survive so a training run naming the
reference still resolves to something that can say what happened to it, and
only the rows are gone.

403.description: Reading rows needs the admin role

410.description: Withdrawn: an erasure took this corpus' rows

get.summary: Every immutable corpus this archive has produced.

post.summary: Erase conversation content, wherever it has reached.
post.description:
Two steps, and the second is the one that is easy to forget: the archive's
content is removed, and then every published corpus that read one of these
conversations has its rows deleted too. Erasing the archive and leaving the
corpus would be an erasure in name only.

What remains everywhere is the record: heads, digests, review decisions and
export manifests. That is what lets an auditor still be told what was there.

get.summary: Every export job, newest first.

post.summary: Queue an export of the archive into an immutable corpus.
post.description:
202, not 201: what comes back is a job, and the corpus it will produce does
not exist yet. A 201 would be this API claiming a dataset that a worker has
not built.

202.description: Queued, or the job this request already started

get.summary: One job: where it is, what it has counted, and what it left out.

post.summary: Stop a job. What it has written stays written; there is no version.

get.summary: What this instance demands before it will hold conversation content.
What was actually said. The one route that leaves the encryption boundary.
get.description:
A turn whose content has been erased answers 410 rather than 404: "it was
here and it is gone" is the answer an auditor came for, and a 404 would make
a completed erasure indistinguishable from a turn that never existed.

403.description: Reading content needs the admin role

410.description: Erased: the head remains, the words do not

post.summary: Approve or reject one turn, attributed to whoever is asking.

get.summary: One conversation's turns. Heads only: nothing here is decrypted.

parameters.name: review
parameters.description: Narrow to one review state — what the review queue asks for.

parameters.name: finding
parameters.description: Narrow to turns carrying a finding of this kind.

post.summary: Record conversation content, with the consent and retention that permit it.

422.description: Refused: every policy problem at once

get.summary: Sessions, each grouping the runs it produced.
get.description:
The level above a run, so the panel can start from "which session" and walk
down to a single LLM call without going back to a flat list and re-filtering.

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description:
Only sessions with activity in the last this-many seconds. See
[`crate::window`].

parameters.name: search
parameters.description:
Substring match on the conversation id. The one control that turns a
long list into the session someone is actually looking for.

get.summary: Every saved Flow PHP recipe, newest save first.

post.summary: Save a content-addressed revision of a Flow PHP recipe.

get.summary: Which hubs are configured, and the variable to set for each that is not.
The bytes of one picture inside a hub dataset.
get.description:
Exists because a hub does not always have an address for its own pictures.
A corpus that keeps them in a `binary` column hands over base64 in the row
and nothing else, so the row a query returns names the *cell* and this
resolves it — which is also what lets the panel draw such a picture at all,
same-origin and with no expiry.

Not cached: it is a preview of somebody else's corpus, and the copy that is
meant to last is the blob an import writes.

parameters.name: row
parameters.description: Which row of the split, counting from zero.

parameters.name: column
parameters.description: Which column of it.

502.description: The hub refused, shortened the cell, or it is not a picture

get.summary: The rows inside one hub dataset.
get.description:
The other half of discovery, and a different question from the search: that
one answers "which corpora exist", this one "what is in this one". An
import built from a search result alone registers a single row pointing at
a web page — the corpus is the *rows*, and until this route existed there
was no way for a pipeline to read them.

It reports the columns the corpus declares and hands the rows over as they
came. Which of them is a picture, what a caption is called and what a
family key is built from are decided in the script, because they are
questions about that corpus rather than about this one.

A hub that cannot answer is a 502 carrying its sentence rather than an
empty list, for the same reason the search route's 501 is not one: "no
rows" is a claim about the corpus, and this is a claim about the request.

parameters.name: dataset
parameters.description: `owner/name`, exactly as a search result addresses it.

parameters.name: hub
parameters.description: Which hub holds it. Only Hugging Face serves rows; see [`Hubs::images`].

parameters.name: config
parameters.description:
The dataset's configuration and split. Both are discovered when absent,
which is the common case — a corpus published as one `train` split has
names nobody should have to look up in order to see it.

parameters.name: address
parameters.description:
Columns to hand over as an address rather than as a value,
comma-separated.

This is where "which column is bytes" is decided, and the caller
decides it. A hub declares a column `binary` and that is the *hub's*
word for a byte string; whether those bytes are a picture, a PDF or an
OCR dump is a question about the corpus, and answering it here would be
answering it for every corpus. A script that names nothing gets every
column as it came.

What the substitution is for is size, not meaning: a column of base64
pictures is megabytes per page, and an address is resolved by
[`Hubs::cell`] only when somebody actually wants the bytes.

502.description: The hub refused, or does not serve rows

get.summary: Search the configured hubs.
get.description:
Always 200 when at least one hub is configured, even if every one of them
failed: the per-hub status carries the failure. A search where Kaggle is
rate-limited and Hugging Face answered is a partial result, and returning a
502 for it would throw away the half that worked.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description:
Free text. Empty asks each hub for its own idea of what is popular,
which is a worse question than any real one but a reasonable landing
state for a search box nobody has typed in yet.

parameters.name: hub
parameters.description: One hub, or both when absent.

get.summary: One immutable dataset version, returned in small slices for an interactive viewer.
Every saved dataset, newest execution first.

post.summary: Persist one completed Flow PHP execution as an immutable dataset version.

get.summary: One dimension's rows: the explorer's top level, whatever it is rooted on.
get.description:
`session`, `agent`, `runtime`, `workflow`, `trace`, `model` and `tool` all
return the same row shape, so the panel's tree has one renderer rather than
one per pivot. See `aiwatcher_projector::dimensions`.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: What to group runs by

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description:
Only runs with activity in the last this-many seconds, before they are
grouped. See [`crate::window`] — a row whose every run falls outside the
window disappears with them rather than staying behind as an empty key.

parameters.name: agent_id
parameters.description:
Narrow to runs that ran this agent, whatever the dimension is. Lets the
tree stay scoped when someone arrives from an agent-filtered view.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description:
Substring match on the key. The one control that turns a long list into
the row someone is looking for.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description:
Cursor: return rows after this key in the current sort order. Keyed
rather than offset, because the list reorders as runs arrive.

get.summary: Which engine this instance can reach, if any.
get.description:
A 501 rather than an empty body when none is configured, so a client can
tell "this deployment has no orchestrator" from "the orchestrator has
nothing to run" — different problems with different fixes.

post.summary: Start one.
post.description:
`202`, not `200`: nothing has run yet. What comes back is an
acknowledgement carrying the engine's reference, a link into its console,
and the `workflow_run_id` the events this execution publishes are expected
to arrive under — which is what lets the panel open a live stream for work
that has not started.

400.description: The engine refused it: an undeclared input, a missing one, a value that will not bind

get.summary: Where one launched execution has got to, as the engine sees it.
get.description:
A second opinion, not the truth: aiwatcher's own view comes from the log
and answers a different question. When they disagree the disagreement is
the finding — an execution the engine calls `succeeded` that published no
events is a producer nobody instrumented.

parameters.name: reference
parameters.description: The reference from a launch, e.g. project:domain:execution

get.summary: One page of what the engine could start.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring over name and description.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description: Overrides the configured project and domain for this request.

parameters.name: stage
parameters.description:
`curation | training | evaluation | inference`. A hint the engine
derived from the entity's name — see `core::engine::PipelineStage`.

parameters.name: token
parameters.description: The engine's own continuation token, from a previous `next_token`.

get.summary: One entity and the inputs it declares.
get.description:
Read again at launch time by the adapter, so this is what a form renders
and never what a launch is validated against — a panel open since before a
redeploy is showing an interface that no longer exists.

parameters.name: workflow_id
parameters.description: An engine reference, e.g. lp:project:domain:name:version

get.summary: Suites: the level above a report, and what MLflow calls an experiment.
get.description:
A separate resource rather than `/evaluations/suites`, so an evaluation
that happens to be called `suites` is still reachable.

get.summary: Evaluation reports, newest first.
get.description:
The other half of the loop the traces come from: a trace says what one run
did, an evaluation says whether the thing producing those runs is getting
better. They arrive on the same log and are folded apart — an `eval.*`
event produces no span and no row in the runs list. See
`aiwatcher_projector::evaluations`.

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description:
Only reports that finished — or, while they are still running, started
— in the last this-many seconds. See [`crate::window`].

parameters.name: search
parameters.description:
Substring over the id, the suite, the dataset, the variant and the
parameter values.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: Cursor: the last evaluation id on the previous page. Exclusive.

get.summary:
One evaluation: its parameters, its metrics, its cases, the document the
producer attached, and the previous evaluation of the same suite on the
same dataset.

parameters.name: evaluation_id
parameters.description: The evaluation to fetch

post.summary: Publish events over HTTP.
post.description:
The fallback path for clients that cannot reach Laser. Returns 403 when the
instance is configured without a sink.

Writer, not viewer: this is the one read-model route that puts something in
the durable log, and an agent that publishes here is a machine identity —
an authentik service account holding a token for this audience, or a
bearer the operator issued. Reading runs and writing them are different
permissions in every deployment that has more than one team.

get.summary: Server-sent events for the whole system: a catch-up marker, then live.
get.description:
This is the panel's Observability transport. It is deliberately separate
from the WebSocket below: the panel only receives here, so EventSource can
own reconnects and `Last-Event-ID` resume without client-side machinery.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description:
Resume point. Usually unnecessary for SSE — the browser sends
`Last-Event-ID` on its own — but explicit here for non-browser clients.

get.summary: A WebSocket for the whole system, or one run.
get.description:
Prefer SSE where the traffic is one-way — it reconnects on its own and
survives proxies better. Use this when the panel needs to send *up* as well:
cancelling a run, approving a tool call, submitting human feedback.

parameters.name: run_id
parameters.description: Follow one run only. Omit to follow everything.

get.summary: Aggregates over the runs the projector still holds.
get.description:
Served from the read model rather than from a metrics backend: the numbers
are a fold over data already in memory, so the page renders with no PromQL
and no dependency on VictoriaMetrics being reachable. The window is bounded
by retention — `window.runs_retained` against `window.retention_limit` tells
a caller whether it is looking at everything or at a truncated tail.

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description: Only runs that started within this many seconds of now.

parameters.name: buckets
parameters.description: Buckets in the timeline. Clamped to 6..=200.

get.summary: Every registered model.

post.summary: Register what a run produced.
post.description:
The provenance — dataset, framework, code — is read from the run rather
than from this request, so a version cannot claim a lineage the run it
names does not have. A version that cannot be promoted is still recorded,
and the reason comes back with it.

get.summary: One model: its versions, its labels, and one version's record.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The model name

parameters.name: version
parameters.description: Omitted resolves `production`, then the newest version.

post.summary: Point a label at a version.
post.description:
The one write here that changes what a service loads next, so it needs
`admin` — and the one the registry itself can refuse: a version with no
held-out measurement, or one trained on a dataset name nobody can
reconstruct, is not promotable however much anybody wants it to be.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The model name

422.description: The version may not be promoted

get.summary: Every prompt in the registry.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Case-insensitive substring over the name, the description and the tags.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: Cursor: the last name on the previous page. Exclusive.

post.summary: Publish a version.
post.description:
Idempotent on the text: `created` is `false` when this exact prompt was
already stored, and the version that comes back is the one that was there,
with its original author and notes intact.

get.summary: One prompt: its labels, its versions, and what happened to it lately.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The prompt to fetch

put.summary: Point a label at a version. `production` is the one an SDK reads.
put.description:
A `PUT`, because moving a label twice to the same version is the same
world as moving it once.

parameters.name: name

parameters.name: label

post.summary: Record an optimisation and store its candidate.
post.description:
The verdict in the response is computed here from the held-out scores and
from what the candidate did to the baseline's variables — it is not read
from the request. An optimiser selected its candidate by maximising the
number it is reporting, which makes it the last thing that should grade it.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The prompt that was optimised

404.description: The baseline version is not in the registry

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The prompt

parameters.name: optimization_id
parameters.description: The optimisation to fetch

post.summary: Re-derive the prompt's index from the objects that are stored.
post.description:
The repair path, exposed because the thing it repairs — a head that lost a
concurrent write — is invisible until somebody notices a version missing
from a list. Labels survive it; a label pointing at a version that is gone
does not.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The prompt to re-index

get.summary: One version, with its text.

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: The prompt

parameters.name: version_id
parameters.description: sha256 of the prompt text

get.summary: List runs, newest first.

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description:
Only runs with activity in the last this-many seconds. See
[`crate::window`] — zero and absent both mean everything.

parameters.name: runtime
parameters.description: Runs produced by this service. See `RunSummary::runtimes`.

parameters.name: trace_id

Runs sharing one trace. Normally one run, but a producer that supplies

parameters.name: model
parameters.description:
Runs that made at least one call to this model.

Matched against the run's spans rather than its summary, because a run

Cursor: return runs older than this one. Keyset pagination, because an
offset shifts under a list that is actively growing.

parameters.name: run_id
parameters.description: The run to fetch

get.summary:
Read from the durable log rather than the read model: this is the audit
view, and it must show what was actually recorded.

parameters.name: run_id
parameters.description: The run to fetch

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: Cursor: the `stream_position` of the last event already seen. Exclusive.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description:
Case-insensitive substring over the event type, agent, span key and the

Applied to the page that was read, not to the whole run: the cost of a

page but has `has_more` set means "keep paging", which is what the

get.description:
The waterfall answers "show me this run". This answers "show me every tool
call slower than two seconds", which is the question asked when the run to
look at is not yet known.

Only spans that ended in the last this-many seconds. See
[`crate::window`].

The filter that turns this list into a hunt for a problem: everything
slower than a threshold, whatever it is.

parameters.name: dataset
parameters.description:
An exact `project@version`, or a bare project name to match every
export of it.

post.summary: Open a training run.
post.description:
Answered before the first epoch on purpose: if this instance is going to
refuse the run, a trainer should find out now rather than after six GPU
hours. Re-opening an already-open run returns it, so a retried start does
not lose the curve it already wrote.

parameters.name: run_id
parameters.description: The run id the trainer chose

parameters.name: run_id
parameters.description: The run id

post.summary: One batch of progress: epochs, sampled points, checkpoints, profiles.
post.description:
Returns the summary rather than the whole record, because a trainer flushing
every epoch does not want its own curve back every time.

parameters.name: run_id
parameters.description: The run id

get.summary: Executions, newest first.

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description:
Only executions with activity in the last this-many seconds. See
[`crate::window`].

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Substring over the execution id, the workflow id and the agents.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: Cursor: the last execution id on the previous page. Exclusive.

get.summary: Server-sent events for one execution: history, a catch-up marker, then live.
get.description:
Scoped by `workflow_run_id` rather than by run, which is what makes a
stage-per-pod workflow watchable: the pod that has not started yet is the
interesting one, and a subscription resolved to today's run ids would never
see it.

parameters.name: workflow_run_id
parameters.description: The execution to follow

parameters.name: from
parameters.description:
Resume point. Usually unnecessary for SSE — the browser sends
`Last-Event-ID` on its own — but explicit here for non-browser clients.

get.summary: Every workflow the projection knows, most recently active first.
get.description:
Includes workflows nothing ever declared: a producer that has been setting
`workflow_id` since before there was a graph to draw still belongs in the
picker, with whatever shape its runs revealed.

parameters.name: window_seconds
parameters.description:
Only graphs with activity in the last this-many seconds. See
[`crate::window`]. A declaration is not evicted by it — the catalog
keeps the shape, the window decides what is shown.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Substring over the id and the name.

parameters.name: after
parameters.description: Cursor: the last workflow id on the previous page. Exclusive.

get.summary: One workflow's declared shape.

parameters.name: workflow_id
parameters.description: The workflow to fetch

post.summary: Ask the configured orchestrator to run this workflow again.
post.description:
`202`, not `200`: nothing has run yet. What comes back is an
acknowledgement, and the evidence that the rerun happened is the events it
publishes onto the same log as everything else.

parameters.name: workflow_id
parameters.description: The workflow to run again

get.summary: The process is running.
The process can serve traffic.
get.description:
Distinct from liveness: a projector replaying a backlog is alive but not
ready, and restarting it would make the replay start over.

channel.description:
The channel it went over, when there is one worth naming: a queue, a
topic, a shared file.

kind.description:
`handoff`, `request`, `response`, `broadcast` — or whatever else a
producer coins. Free text for the same reason `step_type` is.

node.description: The node it was sent from, when the sender was inside one.

confidence.description:
What the producer thought of its own proposal. Present for `model` and
`ocr`, meaningless for `human`.

id.description:
Unique within its revision. Supplied by the client so links can be
drawn before a save, and validated rather than trusted.

links.description: Named references to other instances in this revision.

text.description: What a recogniser read, for a text instance.

AnnotationProject.description: One annotation project: its vocabulary, its split policy, its overrides.

split_overrides.description:
`group_id` to a fixed side, for the houses that have to be in the test
set. Keyed by family for the same reason the hash is.

split_salt.description:
Mixed into the split hash. Changing it re-deals every family, which is
occasionally what you want and never what you want by accident — so it
is stored, and an export records the one it used.

AnnotationRevision.description: One immutable set of shapes for one image.

revision.description:
SHA-256 of the shapes, the schema version and the image. Author, notes
and time are deliberately outside it: two people drawing the same thing
is one revision.

schema_version.description:
The schema these shapes were checked against. An export refuses a
revision drawn under a different vocabulary rather than guessing.

created.description:
False when this exact page was already stored — an acknowledged retry
rather than a second copy of the rows.

total_rows.description: Rows in the whole batch so far.

AppendRowsRequest.description: A page of rows for an already-staged batch.

page.description:
Which page this is, when the caller is numbering them.

Supplying it makes the append idempotent, which is the difference
between a client that can retry and one that has to reconcile. Omitting
it appends at the end, which is what a single-threaded uploader wants.

key_ids.description:
Key ids this deployment can decrypt with, newest first. Never the keys.
Present so an operator can see that a rotation reached this process
before they retire the old key and make everything sealed under it
unreadable.

ArchiveConfig.description:
What this deployment demands of a producer, and which keys it can open.

Answered before anything is sent, on purpose: a producer that discovers the
consent requirement from a 422 has already put a megabyte of content on the
wire, and the panel needs it to render the archive's state rather than an
empty list that looks like "nothing has happened yet".

ArchivePolicy.description:
What this deployment demands, and the only thing here that outranks a
caller.

max_ttl_days.description:
A `ttl_days` above this is clamped rather than refused, and the clamp is
recorded on the turn. Refusing would push a producer to send the number
this deployment happens to accept, which is a worse record than the
truth plus a clamp.

reject_on_finding.description:
Whether the server's own scan refusing content is fatal.

Off by default, and the reason is worth stating: a scanner is a
heuristic, and one that rejects a write throws away the only copy of an
exchange because a hex string looked like a key. A finding always blocks
the *export* — see [`crate::review`] — which is the gate that matters.

ArchivedTurn.description: A turn as the archive holds it: everything except the words.

content_digest.description:
`sha256` of the canonical content. What makes a re-send idempotent, what
a duplicate is detected on, and what an export version is built from.

oneOf.description: Why the content is gone, when it is.

index_shard.description:
Which index shard lists this turn, once one does.

`None` is the window between writing a head and appending its index
entry. A re-send repairs it, which is why this is on the head rather
than being inferred: without it, a retry would find the head present,
skip the append, and leave the turn invisible to every export forever.

parts.description: The shape of the message, with none of it.

retention_clamped.description:
True when this deployment shortened the retention the producer asked
for. Recorded rather than silent: a corpus built under a policy nobody
noticed had changed is the thing an audit is looking for.

Artifact.description:
Something a node produced, by reference.

The bytes stay wherever the producer put them. aiwatcher keeps the pointer
because a pointer is bounded and a floor-plan PDF is not — see the
artifact guardrail in `CLAUDE.md`.

digest.description:
Content hash, when the producer computed one. What makes "the same
artifact as last time" a checkable claim rather than a guess.

ArtifactRef.description: One file a package is made of.

digest.description:
`sha256` of the bytes, lowercase hex. Required, and the reason this
type exists: an address is not an identity.

uri.description:
Where the bytes are. A pointer, like every other artifact in this
workspace — the registry stores no weights.

AttributeDef.description: One typed field on a class.

required.description:
A required attribute is refused when missing, which is what stops a
half-labelled door from reaching a training export.

values.description: The closed vocabulary for [`AttributeKind::Enum`]. Ignored otherwise.

AttributeKind.description: The type of one attribute a class carries.

BestMetric.description: The number a run is judged on.

created.description: False when this exact export already existed.

CausationId.description:
Names the *direct* cause of this event. Roots itself on the correlation id
when nothing seeded it — the same rule Emmett's scope applies.

Checkpoint.description: An opaque resume position in the log.

CheckpointRecord.description: Where the weights went, and what selected them. Never the weights.

metric.description:
What selected it. A checkpoint with no metric is a periodic save; one
with a metric is a decision.

ConsentRecord.description: Who this is about, on what basis, and what that permits.

reference.description:
Where the record lives: a ticket, a policy id, a URL. Free text on
purpose — the shape differs per organisation and a schema here would
only be worked around.

scope.description:
Empty means nothing was permitted, not everything. An export demanding
[`TrainingScope::Train`] excludes it by name.

subject.description:
Whose data this is: an account id, a tenant, `synthetic`. Not a name —
a pseudonymous handle is what makes an erasure request answerable
without the archive holding a second copy of the identity.

oneOf.description:
The model's own reasoning, where a provider exposes it. Its own variant
because most training shapes must *not* include it, and a `Text` part
carrying it would be indistinguishable from the answer.

A call the assistant asked for. `arguments` is the JSON the model
produced, kept verbatim: a re-serialised copy is a different string and
would break the content digest for no reason.

What a producer removed before sending. The digest is of the original,
so a reviewer can tell two different redactions apart, and an export can
exclude a turn whose redaction ate the answer.
Bytes somebody else stored. Never the bytes themselves.

ContentPart.description:
One piece of a message.

A list rather than a string, because a modern turn is not one: an assistant
message can be reasoning, then a tool call, then prose, and a training shape
that has to guess which part was which guesses wrong on the interesting
examples.

[`Self::Reference`] is the guardrail the annotation registry already keeps
for artifacts: a pointer to bytes somebody else stored, never the bytes. An
image or a PDF inlined here would put a file in an archive that is meant to
hold messages, and would put it under an encryption key sized for text.

ContentPolicy.description: Everything a producer asserts about one turn.

oneOf.description:
What the producer's own redaction hook removed. `None` means none ran,
which a protected deployment refuses — see [`ArchivePolicy::check`].

ConversationExclusionReason.description: Why a turn did not reach the corpus.

ConversationExportExclusion.description: One turn that was left out, named.

detail.description: The rule that fired, for a [`ExclusionReason::Finding`].

ConversationExportManifest.description: What a finished export is, forever.

conversations.description:
The conversations this export read, pinned when the job was created.

Kept on the manifest rather than only on the job, because it is what an
erasure searches: "which published corpora hold this person's words" has
to be answerable from the manifests alone.

excluded.description:
A sample of the excluded turns. `excluded_truncated` says whether the
counts above are larger than this list.

oneOf.description: Set when an erasure took this corpus' rows away. The manifest remains.

ConversationExportRequest.description:
What was asked for. The identity of an export, along with the archive's
content at the time.

exclude_findings.description:
Finding kinds that exclude a turn. Defaults to the three that make
content unsafe to train on rather than merely awkward.

require_human_review.description:
Whether a turn nobody approved may be included. Defaults to `true`,
which means "no" — the annotation registry's rule, and the reason the
review queue exists.

required_scope.description:
What the recorded consent has to permit. Defaults to
[`TrainingScope::Train`], the widest of the three.

roles.description:
Roles to include. Empty means every role, which is what a chat shape
wants; a prompt/response shape ignores this and takes what it needs.

ConversationHead.description: One conversation's counts. The review queue reads these and nothing else.

earliest_expiry.description:
The soonest any of this conversation's content expires.

A hint the sweep uses to decide whether to open this conversation at
all, recomputed whenever it does. Being stale costs one wasted read;
being absent would cost a scan of every turn in the archive.

findings.description:
Findings by kind, so "which conversations hold a credential" is a list
rather than a scan.

ungrouped_runs.description:
Runs with no `conversation_id`. They are reachable from the runs list
but have no session to sit under, and silently dropping them would make
the two views disagree about how much exists.

ConversationRole.description:
Who spoke.

`Developer` is separate from `System` because the two have different
retention answers: a developer instruction is the product's own text and a
system prompt may be a customer's. An export can drop one and keep the
other, which it could not do if they were one role.

agents.description: Every agent seen across the conversation's runs, in first-seen order.

last_activity_at.description:
The newest event on any of the session's runs. What the list sorts by,
so an active session stays at the top.

CorrelationId.description: Groups an entire flow. Inherited unchanged by everything the flow causes.

Credential.description:
How the caller proved who they are.

Kept on the identity because the three are not interchangeable when
something goes wrong: a session is a browser, a bearer is a machine, and a
proxy header is a statement by whatever sits in front of this process.

revision.description: SHA-256 of the authored fields. The stable identity of this revision.

DatasetRow.description: One original row and its stable position inside an immutable version.

DatasetRowsPage.description: A small slice suitable for an interactive data viewer.

matching_rows.description: Rows matching the current search across all pages.

total_rows.description: Rows in the immutable artifact before search is applied.

id.description:
Stable slug. What [`crate::integrations::hubs`] matches a mirror
against, and what an import records as the row it was checked against.

items.description: Best published figure. `None` where the authors give a range.

kind.description:
What kind of thing it contains, in the caller's own words —
`floor_plan`, `satellite`, `radiograph`. Free text for the same reason
[`crate::images::ImageRecord::view`] is: an enum here would be one
domain's list.

labels.description: What it labels, in whatever vocabulary the corpus uses.

verified_on.description:
When somebody last read the licence at `url`.

The field that makes a row worth more than a guess, and the one that
goes stale. A row with no date is a row nobody checked.

versions.description: Newest first. Kept in the head so listing does not read every artifact.

DimensionKind.description: What the tree is rooted on.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `after` to fetch the next page. Absent on the last page.

total.description: Rows matching the filter, before the page limit.

ungrouped_runs.description:
Runs that carry no key for this dimension. They are reachable from the
runs list but have no row to sit under, and silently dropping them would
make the two views disagree about how much exists.

DimensionSummary.description: One row of the tree's top level, whatever the dimension is.

agents.description: Every agent seen across the row's runs, in first-seen order.

last_activity_at.description:
The newest event on any of the row's runs. What the list sorts by, so a
row where something is happening stays at the top.

Read from the runs' last event rather than from their start, which is
what it used to be: a row whose runs all began an hour ago and are
still working is active, and sorting it below a row that started one
run a minute ago and finished it buried the thing worth looking at.

running_last_event_at.description:
The newest event on a run in this row that has **not** ended. Absent
when none is running.

What tells a row that is working from a row that stopped talking. The
running count alone cannot: a run whose producer was killed keeps that
count above zero forever, and a spinner that never stops is the one
thing this view must not show without saying how long it has been
spinning. Where to draw the line is the reader's, so the number is
reported rather than judged.

EngineDescription.description: How this instance is wired, for a client deciding what to render.

console_url.description:
The engine's console, when one is configured, so the panel can link out
rather than pretending to be it.

kind.description: `flyte` today. A name, not a version: the panel branches on nothing.

EngineExecution.description:
Where an execution has got to, as the engine sees it.

aiwatcher's own view of a run comes from the log and says something
different: `RunStatus` is what the *producer* reported. When they disagree
the disagreement is the finding — an execution the orchestrator calls
`Failed` whose events stop mid-run is a pod that was killed, and one it
calls `Succeeded` with no events at all is a producer that is not
instrumented.

workflow_run_id.description: Read back from the execution's labels, when aiwatcher set one.

EngineParameter.description:
The shape of one declared input, for a form to render.

Display only. Whatever a caller sends is bound to the engine's *own*
declared type at launch time, read from the engine at that moment — see
[`WorkflowEngine::launch`]. A panel that has been open since before a
redeploy is therefore rendering a stale form against a fresh interface, and
the launch fails with the engine's own message rather than binding a value
to a type nobody checked.

default.description:
The default, rendered as JSON. `None` means there is none, which for a
required parameter is the normal case.

enum_values.description:
The permitted values, when the engine declared a closed set. Turns a
text box into a select, which is the difference between a filter
somebody types wrong and one they pick.

required.description:
Required *and* without a default. A parameter with a default is
optional however the engine phrases it.

type_name.description:
The engine's own name for the type, for the cases [`ParameterKind`]
flattens: a blob, a structured dataset, a union. Shown beside the
field so a `Json` box is not a mystery.

EngineWorkflow.description: One thing a caller could start.

active.description:
Whether the engine considers this version launchable. An inactive
launch plan is listed rather than hidden, because "it is there and it
is switched off" is the answer somebody is looking for when they cannot
find it.

id.description: [`EngineRef::render`] — what `POST /launches` and the detail route take.

name.description: The registered name, without project or domain.

oneOf.description: A guess, never a fact — see [`PipelineStage`].

url.description: Where to see it in the engine's own console, when one is configured.

EntityKind.description:
The kind of registered thing a launch names.

Flyte's launchable unit is a launch plan; a task and a workflow are
registered entities that a launch plan points at. Other engines divide this
differently, so the kind travels with the reference rather than being
assumed.

EpochRecord.description: One epoch: the grain a human reads a training run at.

steps.description:
Optimiser steps inside this epoch. Counted by the client, never sent
one by one — a step is arithmetic, not a request.

ErasureBody.description:
An erasure request: a subject, or a whole conversation.

A POST rather than a DELETE, because it is a request somebody files with a
body and gets a report back — and because the subject it names is personal
data that has no business in a URL. Exactly one of the two fields.

subject.description:
The consent subject, as recorded on the turns. What a person's request
actually names.

ErasureReport.description: What a sweep or an erasure removed.

already_erased.description:
Turns whose retention had run out but whose content was already gone.
Counted so a repeated sweep is visibly a no-op rather than silently one.

corpora_withdrawn.description:
Published corpora whose rows this erasure took away.

The half of an erasure that is easy to forget: erasing the archive and
leaving the corpus is an erasure in name only. Their manifests survive,
so a training run naming one still resolves to something that can say
what happened to it.

ErrorBody.description: The body every error response carries.

code.description: Stable machine-readable discriminator. Switch on this, not on `message`.

details.description:
One line per problem, where a request can fail in more than one way at
once. An annotation is the case that needs it: a labeller fixing one
error per round trip stops using the tool, so every problem in a
drawing is reported together. Absent everywhere else, which keeps the
one JSON shape one shape.

reason.description:
Why the scorer said what it said. A score without its rationale is not
reviewable, which is the whole complaint about opaque eval numbers.

EvaluationComparison.description: This evaluation against the one before it.

fixed.description: Failed on the baseline, passes now.

metrics.description:
Every metric either side reported, so one that appeared or disappeared
is visible rather than silently absent.

regressed.description:
Passed on the baseline, fails now. The view that has to be read before
a release.

EvaluationDetail.description: One evaluation, with everything retained for it.

cases_truncated.description:
More cases were scored than are listed. `summary.cases_total` is still
the true count.

oneOf.description: Against the previous evaluation of the same suite on the same dataset.

report.description:
Whatever the producer put in `data.report` — the free-form half, and
the reason `log_dict` had nowhere to go before this existed.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `after` to fetch the next page. Absent on the last page.

EvaluationStatus.description:
Where an evaluation got to.

The same three states a run has, for the same reason: a report that never
arrived and a report that failed are different facts.

EvaluationSummary.description: One row in the evaluations list.

dataset.description:
The cases it was measured on, ideally versioned. Without this a
comparison is not one; see [`EvaluationDetail::comparison`].

evaluation_id.description:
The producer's `run_id`. An evaluation is an execution too, so it gets
its own stream in the log and its own partition — which is what keeps a
report's events in order without serialising it behind agent traffic.

params.description: Everything that was held fixed, stringified. MLflow's `log_params`.

pass_rate.description:
From the cases where there are any, from `metrics.pass_rate` where the
producer only reported the aggregate.

report_bytes.description: Size of the report document as it arrived, whether or not it was kept.

report_dropped.description:
The document is not held. Either it was over
[`EvaluationConfig::max_report_bytes`] — half a JSON document is not a
JSON document, so it is dropped rather than cut — or it was shed to
keep the projection inside its budget. `report_bytes` still says how
big it was.

suite.description:
What was measured. Falls back through `suite`, `suite_name`, `run_name`
— MLflow's word — and finally the evaluation id, so a producer porting
a `start_run(run_name=…)` call lands somewhere sensible without
renaming anything.

variant.description:
What was under test: a prompt version, a model, a checkout. The join to
the experiments side.

conversation_id.description: Groups several runs a user would think of as one conversation.

data.description:
Type-specific payload. Kept as free-form JSON so an SDK can add a field
without a backend release.

oneOf.description:
Deduplication key. Generated by the ingest edge when absent, which
means a producer that omits it gets at-least-once *without*
deduplication — say so in the SDK docs.

occurred_at.description:
When the producer observed it. Distinct from `ingested_at`, which the
ingest edge stamps — the gap between them is producer lag.

run_id.description: One execution of an agent. This is what a trace is scoped to.

schema_version.description:
Contract version. An envelope from the future is rejected rather than
silently half-read.

sequence.description:
Producer-side counter within the run. Gaps here mean lost events; it is
the only way to notice a producer that dropped a batch.

workflow_id.description:
Which orchestration this run is an execution of.

A conversation groups runs by *who* is talking; a workflow groups them
by *what* is being executed. The same workflow runs across many
sessions, which is the comparison — this graph, before and after a
change — that `conversation_id` cannot express.

workflow_run_id.description:
One execution of that orchestration.

`workflow_id` names the graph; this names the traversal of it. They are
separate because an execution can outlive a run: a stage-per-pod
orchestrator gives every stage its own process and therefore its own
`run_id`, and without this field there is nothing joining the four runs
of one import back into one graph.

Defaulted rather than required — see [`Self::workflow_run`]. A producer
that runs a whole workflow in one process never has to set it.

EventPage.description: One page of a run's history, filtered.

next_cursor.description: Pass as `after` to fetch the next page. Absent at the end of the run.

scanned.description:
Events read before filtering. With a `q`, the difference between this
and `events.len()` is what the filter removed — without it the panel
cannot tell "nothing matched" from "nothing left".

EventType.description:
Every event type aiwatcher understands, plus a passthrough for the
ones it does not.

[`EventType::Unknown`] is deliberate: a producer running a newer SDK
must not have its events rejected. They are stored and streamed
live, they simply take part in no span.

ExclusionReason.description:
Why an image is not in an export.

Every one of these is listed by name in the manifest rather than silently
dropped. An export that quietly loses a third of a corpus reads exactly
like one that did not.

ExecutionDetail.description: One execution, with everything needed to draw it.

edges.description: The declared edges of the workflow this executes.

messages.description:
Messages actually observed. Never merged with `edges`: sequence is not
communication, and a view that conflated them would claim a handoff
that nothing recorded.

messages_truncated.description:
Older messages were shed under memory pressure. The count in
`summary.messages` is still complete.

nodes.description: In declaration order where declared, then first-seen order for the rest.

ExecutionStatus.description: Where a whole traversal got to.

ExecutionSummary.description: One row in the executions list.

agents.description: Every agent seen anywhere in the traversal, in first-seen order.

last_activity_at.description:
The newest event folded into this execution, ended or not.

An execution outlives its runs, and a stage-per-pod one is idle between
them by design, so "started three hours ago" says nothing about whether
anything is still moving. This does. Same fact as `RunSummary`'s field
of the same shape, and it is what the time window matches on.

last_checkpoint.description:
The newest checkpoint folded into this row, so a client can resume the
live stream from here without re-reading the execution.

runs.description:
The runs this traversal is made of. One for a single-process workflow,
one per stage for a stage-per-pod one.

instances_per_class.description: Class to instance count, over the whole export.

instances_per_class_split.description:
Class to per-split instance counts. This is the table that says the test
set contains four doors, which is the number that invalidates a recall
figure before anybody quotes it.

ExportFormat.description: The shape a row is written in.

ExportIndex.description: Which versions of one name exist.

ExportJob.description: A resumable export, as it sits in the store.

claimed_by.description:
The worker currently holding this job: a pod name in a cluster.

Not an owner — a lease. It expires, which is what lets a job survive the
process that was running it, and it is re-checked at every shard, which
is what stops the process it outlived from writing beside its
replacement.

conversations.description: The conversations this job will read, resolved once and never re-read.

cursor.description: How many of them are already in a written shard. The resume point.

version.description: The immutable reference, once there is one.

claimed_by.description:
Which worker holds it, while one does. Answers "why has this been
running for twenty minutes" without opening a log.

classes.description:
In schema order. The index in this list is the category id COCO uses,
which is why the order is fixed by the schema and not by first sight.

export.description:
SHA-256 of everything below except `created_at` and `note`. Two exports
of an unchanged project are one export.

classes.description: Empty means every class in the schema.

require_human_review.description:
Refuse an image whose accepted revision was produced entirely by a model
or an import. Defaults to on, because that is the whole point of
recording an origin.

split_salt.description: Overrides the project's salt for this export only.

oneOf.description: Overrides the project's ratios for this export only.

views.description:
Which [`views`](crate::images::ImageRecord::view) to include.

Empty means every one, which is the right default for a corpus that
has only one kind of picture — most of them. A corpus that mixes kinds
names the ones a model reads, and every other image is excluded *by
name* in the manifest rather than quietly.

ExportSample.description:
One image in an export, pinned to the revision that was accepted when the
export was built.

rights.description:
Flattened for the manifest so a reader can see the licence mix without
resolving every image.

conversations.description:
Named explicitly. Empty means every conversation in the archive, which
is the common case and the one that needs the window below.

since.description: Only conversations last active at or after this moment.

withdrawn.description: True once an erasure has taken this corpus' rows away.

Finding.description: One problem, located but not quoted.

found_by.description: Who found it: `scanner`, or a reviewer's identity.

part.description:
Which content part, by index. `None` for a finding about the turn as a
whole — a duplicate, a policy gap.

rule.description:
The rule that fired: `email`, `aws-access-key-id`, or a reviewer's own
word when a human recorded it.

start.description:
Byte offset and length inside that part's text. Enough for the review
UI to highlight it once the content is decrypted, and useless to anyone
who only has the head.

FindingKind.description: What kind of problem a finding is.

oneOf.description:
Renamed for the same reason [`GeometryKind::BBox`] is: the derived
snake_case of `BBox` is `b_box`.

holes.description:
Interior rings. A room with a chimney is one polygon with one hole,
not two polygons whose difference a consumer has to infer.

GeometryKind.description:
The shape a class is drawn as.

One kind per class, checked on save. A class drawn as a polygon in one
image and a box in another produces a training target nothing can decode.

HubColumn.description:
One column a hub dataset declares, in the hub's own words.

Carried verbatim and not interpreted. aiwatcher does not know which column
of somebody else's corpus is the picture, what the caption is called, or
whether `indices` is an id or a label — and a route that decided would be
deciding it for every corpus. This is what a script is written against.

kind.description: The hub's type tag: `Image`, `Value`, `Sequence`, and so on.

HubDataset.description:
One dataset a hub says it has.

Every field here is the hub's, not aiwatcher's, with two exceptions:
[`usage`](Self::usage) and [`curated_source`](Self::curated_source), which
this module decides — see `Hubs::reconcile`.

claimed_license.description:
What the *hub* says the licence is. Named for what it is.

Empty is common and is not a licence: an unstated licence on a mirror
means nobody filled the field in, never that the data is unencumbered.

curated_source.description:
The id of the [`DatasetSource`] row this matched, when it matched one.

A match is on the *original's* URL, so it means "a human read this
licence, at the source, on a date" — which is the only thing that ever
justifies a usage other than unclear.

id.description: `owner/name` on both hubs, which is also how each addresses a download.

usage.description:
Always [`SourceUsage::Unclear`] unless [`curated_source`](Self::curated_source)
is set. This is the guardrail, expressed as a field that cannot say
"commercial" on a hub's word.

HubFile.description:
One file inside a hub dataset, as far as the hub will say.

Only enough to tell a floor-plan corpus from a CSV of house prices before
downloading either. Sizes are the hub's own and are not verified.

HubKind.description: Which mirror a row came from.

HubRow.description: One row of a hub dataset, as the hub sent it.

omitted.description:
Columns left out, and why they would have been.

Named, because a column that is simply absent reads as a column the
corpus does not have.

row.description:
Every column, under the corpus's own name for it.

Two substitutions, and both are about size rather than meaning: a cell
the hub sent as bytes becomes a path back into this process that
resolves them (see [`Hubs::cell`]), because a hundred rows of base64 is
a result heavier than the pictures it describes; and a cell too large
to carry is left out and named in [`omitted`](Self::omitted).

row_index.description:
Where it sat in the split. The only name a row has that the corpus did
not choose, and the one a family key is usually built from.

HubRowsPage.description: One page of a hub dataset's rows.

columns.description: What the corpus declares it holds. A script is written from this.

config.description:
Resolved, never echoed: what was actually read, which is what makes the
same call repeatable after a dataset gains a second split.

total_rows.description: The split's own count, when the hub reports one.

HubSearchPage.description: A page of results, and what each hub had to say about answering.

notice.description:
Repeated on every response rather than left to a tooltip, because it is
the one thing a reader of this list has to know about it.

HubStatus.description: Whether a hub answered, and if not, why.

error.description:
Present when the hub was asked and did not answer. A search with one
hub down is a partial answer, and saying which half is missing beats
both an error and a silently short list.

results.description: Rows this hub contributed to the page.

variable.description: What to set when `configured` is false.

HubsPage.description: What this instance can search, before anybody types a query.

notice.description:
The same sentence every search response carries. Repeated here so a
panel that renders the hub list before the first search has it.

HumanFinding.description:
A finding a person recorded.

Deliberately narrower than [`Finding`]: no byte offsets, because a reviewer
is describing a judgement rather than a match, and no `found_by`, because
the registry fills that in from the caller's identity. A client that could
name its own reviewer could file somebody else's approval.

expires_at.description:
When this identity stops being valid, as a Unix timestamp. `None` for
the anonymous identity, which never expires because it was never
issued.

groups.description:
What the provider asserted, verbatim. Kept beside the resolved roles so
an operator debugging "why is this person only a viewer" can see the
input to the mapping rather than guessing at it.

roles.description: The roles the groups above resolved to, highest last.

subject.description:
The provider's stable identifier — `sub` on an OIDC token. Never the
email, which people change.

oneOf.description: The shapes of one revision — the accepted one, or the one asked for.

split.description:
Which side of the split this image's family is on, under the project's
current policy. Shown so a labeller knows whether they are drawing a
test case, which changes how carefully they draw it.

ImageDetail.description: Where one image's revisions and its head are read together.

ImageHead.description:
One image's mutable head: what it is, what has been drawn on it, and which
of those drawings is the truth.

accepted.description: The revision an export reads. Set only by acceptance.

group_id.description: The split key. Every rendering of one building shares it.

image_id.description:
SHA-256 of the bytes, lowercase hex. Computed by the server on upload
and never taken from the client.

level.description:
`ground_floor`, `attic`, `basement`. Free text, because the vocabulary
differs per supplier and guessing it wrong is worse than keeping theirs.

metadata.description:
Everything known about this plan that did not come from the pixels: the
room names and areas from the catalogue page, the plan's own dimensions,
the listing URL.

This is the field that makes OCR a cross-check rather than a source.

source.description: Where it came from — a supplier, a public corpus, a scan batch.

uri.description: Where the bytes are. `blob:<image_id>` for something uploaded here.

view.description:
What kind of picture this is, in the caller's own words.

Free text for the same reason `level` is: the vocabulary differs per
corpus, and an enum shipped here would be one project's list imposed on
every other. An export selects the views it wants by name, so a corpus
that mixes photographs with diagrams, or plans with elevations, keeps
the ones a model reads out of the ones it does not — by saying so
rather than by somebody remembering.

bytes_stored.description: Bytes stored. The number that answers "why is the bucket bigger".

fetched.description: Rows whose bytes this job downloaded and stored.

ImportJob.description: A resumable import, as it sits in the store.

cursor.description:
Pages already registered *and* whose result shard is stored. The resume
point.

pages.description: Pages this job will read, pinned when it was created.

reject_pages.description:
Pages that wrote a reject shard, so reading them is a seek rather than
a scan of every page of a million-row import.

rows.description:
Rows across those pages. The denominator a progress bar may use,
because it was counted rather than guessed.

shards.description:
One per finished page: what was registered, hashed. The version
material.

warnings.description:
Things that are not errors and that somebody has to read anyway.

Always present, even when empty: a client that has to distinguish
"no warnings" from "the field is missing" is a client with a bug
waiting in it.

ImportJobRequest.description: What a job was asked to do.

batch.description: The staged batch to read. Sealed by queueing, so its rows are pinned.

dry_run.description:
Check every row and register nothing.

It still downloads: a row with no content address is refused by the
registry, so a dry run that skipped the fetch would reject every row
and teach the reader nothing about the batch. Blobs are addressed by
their content, so a dry run followed by a real import stores each
picture once.

ImportManifest.description: What a finished import is, forever.

batch_digest.description:
The batch's own content address. Two manifests naming the same one read
the same rows.

fetched.description:
Rows whose bytes were downloaded from a hub and stored here.

Set by the caller that did the downloading, not by the import: this
module writes an object store and reaches nothing. Zero for a batch
whose pipeline had already stored its own bytes, which is every batch
that carries an `image_id`.

warnings.description:
Things that are not errors and that somebody has to read anyway.

Every one of these describes a state where the import succeeds and the
resulting corpus is quietly worth less than it looks.

dry_run.description:
Check everything and register nothing.

The default is false, but the panel always asks for a dry run first:
six hundred rows with a group key mapped from the filename is not
something anybody wants to discover after it is in the project.

evidence.description:
Who checked that assertion, where, and when. Recorded, never enforced —
see [`RightsEvidence`].

rights.description:
What the caller asserts may be done with every image in this batch.

One value for the batch rather than per row, because a licence is a
property of the corpus and a per-row field invites a pipeline to derive
it from a column — which is exactly the mirror's word, laundered
through a `withEntry`.

ImportRow.description:
One image a pipeline produced.

Deliberately the same field names as [`RegisterImageRequest`], minus what
the request supplies once for the whole batch. A Flow query that renames
its columns to these is the entire mapping layer.

group_id.description: The **building**, not the drawing. See the module docstring.

image_id.description:
SHA-256 of the bytes, when the pipeline has already fetched and stored
them. Absent for a row that only points at a remote file.

ImportSource.description: Where a batch came from, recorded on every image it produces.

claimed_license.description:
What the hub said the licence was. Kept verbatim and never believed —
it is evidence about the mirror, not about the data.

config.description:
The configuration and split the rows came from. `default`/`train` is
the common shape and not the only one, and a corpus whose `test` split
was imported as if it were `train` is a leak nothing downstream can
see.

curated_source.description:
The curated row this matched, if any. The presence of this is what lets
[`check_rights`] refuse an over-claim.

oneOf.description: The curated verdict, when there was one.

files.description:
The files this batch was read out of, with whatever digest the hub
stated for each.

The hub's word, kept as the hub's word — like `claimed_license`, and
unlike the per-image content address, which is computed here from bytes
this process hashed. Both are worth having: one says what the mirror
thinks it is serving, the other says what actually arrived.

hub.description:
`kaggle` or `huggingface`, or anything else for a pipeline that did not
start at a hub.

pipeline.description:
The Flow PHP that produced these rows. Provenance that survives the
import: "where did these six hundred images come from" has an answer
that is a script rather than a memory.

revision.description:
The commit the rows were read at.

A dataset id is a moving target: `main` is whatever the uploader
pushed last, so a corpus re-read a month later is a different corpus
under the same name — and a training run naming it is naming nothing
anybody can go back to. This is the field that makes "the images this
model learned from" a question with an answer.

Empty when the hub did not report one, which is recorded rather than
invented: a blank revision says the provenance is a name, and a made-up
one would say it is a commit.

events.description:
A batch. Publishing several events in one call is what keeps a chatty
producer from paying a round trip per token.

last_checkpoint.description:
The checkpoint of the last event written. A client can hand this to the
live stream to pick up exactly where its own write landed.

Keypoint.description: One named position inside a keypoint instance.

visible.description:
False when the plan shows the element but not this position — a door
whose leaf is drawn open past the page edge still has a hinge.

color.description:
What the canvas draws it in. Presentation only; nothing downstream may
depend on it.

ignore.description:
Excluded from every training target and from the loss.

The furniture, the hatching and the title block are not background —
they are pixels a model must not be scored on either way. Marking them
is cheaper than labelling them and far cheaper than the false positives
they produce.

keypoints.description:
The named positions a [`GeometryKind::Keypoints`] class expects, in the
order the tool asks for them.

layer.description:
Which grid this class paints into when a revision is rasterised.

The generic form of a problem that does not look generic: some classes
*overlay* others and must not erase them. An opening in a wall, a
defect on a component, a marking on a road — in every case the thing
underneath is still there, and one grid could only represent the
overlay by deleting it.

So the schema says so. Classes on the same layer share one integer grid
and paint in declaration order, last wins; classes on different layers
never contend, and a model reads one head per layer. Most vocabularies
need exactly one layer and never set this.

links.description:
Named references this class may hold to other instances in the same
image: `wall` for an opening, `connects` for a door's two rooms.

name.description:
Stable machine name — `wall_exterior`, not `Exterior wall`. Renaming it
is a new schema version, never an edit.

optional_keypoints.description:
Keypoints that may be left out because the plan does not show them.
Everything else in `keypoints` is required.

LabelSchema.description:
The complete, versioned vocabulary of one project.

Content-addressed like everything else authored here: the version is the
digest of the classes, so an unchanged schema re-saved is the same version
and a renamed class is unmistakably a different one.

step.description: Per step — retrieval, embedding, rerank and the rest.

time_to_first_token.description: Time to first token, from the `gen_ai.first_token` span event.

LaunchAccepted.description: What came back. Not a result — nothing has finished.

reference.description: The engine's name for the execution it just created.

workflow_run_id.description:
Echoed back so the caller can subscribe to
`/api/v1/workflow-executions/{id}/stream` immediately — before the
producer has published anything, which is the interesting part of a
launch's first thirty seconds.

LaunchBody.description:
What a caller may ask to start.

Note what is not here, and it is the same absence as `RerunBody`: no
endpoint, no image, no command. `deny_unknown_fields` so an attempt to
supply one is a 400 rather than a field that is silently ignored and reads
as accepted.

inputs.description: Parameter name to value, bound to the types the engine declares.

workflow.description:
The engine reference from the catalog, e.g.
`lp:planner:production:house_dataset_curation:v7`.

workflow_run_id.description:
Supply one to join this execution to events a producer will publish
under an id it already knows. Left out, aiwatcher mints one and returns
it, which is what the panel follows.

LawfulBasis.description:
What makes keeping this lawful, in the producer's own words.

aiwatcher cannot check any of it and does not pretend to. What it can do is
refuse to hold content that never claimed one, and record the claim
verbatim so that an auditor asking "why was this row eligible" gets the
answer somebody actually gave rather than one reconstructed afterwards.

LinkDef.description: One named reference from an instance to another instance.

min.description:
How many targets this link must have. `(1, 1)` for an opening's wall,
`(2, 2)` for the two spaces it connects.

targets.description: Classes the target may belong to. Empty means any class.

LiveEvent.description:
What a browser receives over SSE or WebSocket.

Kept small on purpose: the panel gets the event as it happened, not a
re-derived projection, and `checkpoint` is what a reconnecting client sends
back as `Last-Event-ID`.

workflow_id.description:
Carried for the same reason `conversation_id` is: the live channel is
filtered server-side, and a subscriber watching one workflow execution
cannot be served by resolving it to a set of run ids at subscribe time —
a stage that starts *after* the browser connected would be filtered out
by the set it was given.

oneOf.description: A replayed or live event.
The replay is finished; everything after this is live.

The requested cursor was too old to replay from memory and the log was
read instead. Surfaced so the panel can say so rather than pretend the
stream was continuous.

LiveFrame.description:
A frame in the live stream.

`Caught` is not decoration: it is what lets the panel switch from "loading
history" to "live" at the right moment, instead of guessing from a timeout.
It mirrors Emmett's `MessageSourceCaughtUp` control message.

redirect_url.description:
Where to send the browser to end the session at the provider too.
`None` when the provider declares no `end_session_endpoint`, in which
case clearing the cookie is all a sign-out can do.

MessageId.description:
Unique id of a single event, used for deduplication.

Generated as a UUIDv7 when the producer does not supply one; ULIDs and any
other sortable opaque string are accepted on the wire.

MessageKind.description:
Emmett splits messages into commands and events; aiwatcher only ingests
events today, but the discriminator is on the wire from day one so adding
control commands later is not a breaking change.

delta.description:
`current - baseline`, and `None` when either side is missing — a
missing metric is not a delta of zero.

runs_retained.description:
Runs the read model holds in total. A `runs_considered` well below this
means the filter is narrow; the two being equal *and* at the retention
cap means older runs have been evicted and the window is truncated.

ModelDetail.description:
One model, its head and one version's full record.

`head` is a field rather than a flattened one, unlike the annotation
registry's equivalent. Flattening reads better in the JSON and produces a
TypeScript intersection type that the panel then cannot narrow, so the
nesting is the price of the client being generated rather than written.

ModelHead.description:
One model's mutable head: its versions, newest first, and its labels.

Labels live here and nowhere else, exactly as a prompt's do: a version is
immutable and `production` is not.

labels.description: Label to version id. `production` is the one a deployment reads.

ModelMetrics.description:
What a version measured, split by which data measured it.

Two maps rather than one, because the distinction is the whole point.
`validation` is what the training loop watched and selected against;
`test` is what nothing was allowed to look at. A registry that merged them
would let a model be promoted on the number its own early stopping
maximised.

ModelPackage.description: Everything a serving runtime needs and is not allowed to guess.

artifacts.description: Every file, each with its digest. At least one.

dependencies.description:
Package name to version specifier. What has to be present for the
entry point to import.

entry_point.description:
What inside the package to load: a file name, a module path, a
`module:function`. Interpreted by the loader for that runtime and by
nothing else.

preprocessing.description:
What the trainer did to its inputs, in its own words: `resize:512`,
`normalize:imagenet`, `edge-grid:8`.

Free text and deliberately not executable. A package that shipped
